docs.title: 🤖 FLL Robot Simulator
docs.text:
Welcome to the documentation for FLL Robot Simulator (fll-sim), an open-source, web-first 3D physics robotics simulator designed specifically for FIRST LEGO League (FLL) teams, coaches, mentors, and students.

       ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │               FLL Robot Simulator (WebGL)              │
       │                                                        │
       │   BrickLink Studio (.io) / LDraw (.ldr) CAD Models     │
       │                           ▼                            │
       │         Topological Pin Clustering Pre-Solver          │
       │                           ▼                            │
       │         Rapier3D Physics Engine (Wasm, 60Hz)           │
       │                           ▼                            │
       │          Asynchronous SPIKE Prime Python VM            │
       │                           ▼                            │
       │           Three.js 3D Viewport & HUD Telemetry         │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Why FLL Robot Simulator?
docs.text:
FIRST LEGO League teams commonly face major hurdles when preparing competition robots: * Hardware Bottlenecks: Only one physical robot is available per team, forcing students to wait in line for testing time. * Lack of Modern Simulators: Legacy desktop simulators (such as Virtual Robotics Toolkit) are proprietary desktop abandonware with closed ecosystems. Web alternatives either lack physics or are restricted to rigid 2D grid worlds. * Physics Engine Overload: Simulating hundreds of individual Technic friction pins and beams in real-time crashes standard physics solvers.

FLL Robot Simulator solves these challenges: 1. Zero-Install WebGL: Runs directly in Chrome, Edge, Safari, or Firefox on laptops and Chromebooks. 2. True LEGO CAD Integration: Ingests real models from BrickLink Studio (.io) and LeoCAD (.ldr). 3. Compound Pin Clustering: Pre-solves static pin-and-beam connections, fusing 120+ static parts into compound rigid bodies while preserving active 1-DOF joints (wheels, attachment arms). 4. Authentic SPIKE Prime Python Runtime: Write standard Python using PrimeHub, MotorPair, and ColorSensor. Run line followers, gyro turns, and precision drive missions in simulation before touching the real robot!

docs.title: Architecture & Engineering Design
docs.text: This document details the software architecture, physical simulation pipeline, kinematic solver, and mathematical models behind fll-sim.

docs.title: 1. System Architecture
docs.text:
The simulator is structured into six strictly decoupled layers with unidirectional data flow:

flowchart TD

    SpikeVM --> MotorCtrl["Motor Velocity & PID Controller"]
    MotorCtrl --> RapierPhysics["Rapier3D Physics Engine (60Hz Wasm)"]
    RapierPhysics --> SensorSim["Virtual Sensor Manager (Raycasting)"]

    SensorSim --> Telemetry["Live Telemetry Stream"]
    Telemetry --> HUD["DOM HUD Dashboard"]
    Viewport3D --> HUD

docs.title: The Challenge of LEGO Physics
docs.text:
A typical FLL competition robot consists of 300 to 600 pieces: * 100+ Technic friction pins (2780, 6558, 32054) * Dozens of liftarms, beams, and frames * Hub, battery, and motors * Wheels and attachments

If each pin and beam is simulated as an independent rigid body connected by physics joints, the constraint solver faces thousands of simultaneous equations. The simulation quickly lags, collapses, or explodes.

docs.title: The Clustering Pre-Solver Solution
docs.text:
fll-sim analyzes the connectivity graph before handing geometry to Rapier3D: 1. Catalog Classification: Every part is tagged by role: FASTENER_PIN, STRUCTURAL_BEAM, CHASSIS_CORE, MOTOR_STATOR, MOTOR_ROTOR, or WHEEL_RIM. 2. Graph Connected Components: All parts connected by rigid friction pins are merged into an equivalence class. 3. Compound Body Generation: Each connected component becomes one Rapier rigid body equipped with an array of primitive colliders (boxes, cylinders, spheres). 4. Joint Identification: Only active degrees of freedom (axles seated in motor stators, free-spinning wheel hubs) are converted into Rapier 1-DOF Revolute Joints.

As a result, a 400+ part robot collapses into \(\le 4\) rigid bodies: * Body 0: Main Chassis (Hub, battery, frame, sensors, fixed motor stators) * Body 1: Left Drive Wheel * Body 2: Right Drive Wheel * Body 3: Rear Caster Skid

docs.title: 3.1 Wheel Kinematics & Degrees
docs.text:
For an FLL robot with wheel diameter \(D = 56\text{ mm}\): $\(C = \pi \cdot D \approx 17.593\text{ cm}\)$

To drive a linear distance \(d\) in centimeters: $\(\Delta \theta = \left(\frac{d}{\pi \cdot D}\right) \times 360^\circ\)$

For differential drive steering: $\(\text{Speed}_{\text{left}} = V \cdot \left(1 - \frac{2 \cdot \max(0, -S)}{100}\right)\)$ $\(\text{Speed}_{\text{right}} = V \cdot \left(1 - \frac{2 \cdot \max(0, S)}{100}\right)\)$ where \(S \in [-100, 100]\) is the steering value.

docs.title: 3.2 Gyro Yaw Angle Extraction
docs.text: The robot's heading yaw \(\theta\) is extracted directly from the chassis rigid body quaternion \(q = (x, y, z, w)\): $\(\theta = \text{atan2}\left(2(wy - zx),\, 1 - 2(y^2 + x^2)\right) \times \frac{180}{\pi}\)$

docs.title: 3.3 Sensor UV Projection & Reflected Light
docs.text: Color sensors cast a downward ray from \((X_0, Y_0, Z_0)\) rotated by the chassis yaw to find the mat intersection point \((X_{\text{mat}}, Z_{\text{mat}})\). The coordinates are mapped to normalized texture coordinates: $\(u = \frac{X_{\text{mat}} + L/2}{L}, \quad v = \frac{Z_{\text{mat}} + W/2}{W}\)$ Reflected light is computed via human perceived luminance: $\(\text{Reflected Light \%} = \text{round}\left(\frac{0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B}{255} \times 100\right)\)$

docs.title: Module Boundaries & Invariants
docs.text:
1. src/cad/: Pure data structures and graph algorithms. Must not import from three, Rapier, or DOM APIs.
  2. src/physics/: Pure physics engine logic. Must run in headless Node/Vitest environments without a browser window.
  3. src/runtime/: Pure asynchronous execution logic. Exposes promises that resolve when physical movement completes.
  4. src/view/: WebGL rendering layer. Synchronizes Three.js visual meshes from read-only physics state.

docs.title: 4. Quality Gates & Testing Standards
docs.text:
Every change must pass: 

make test && make build && make spec-validate && make docs-build
No broken tests, type errors, or spec validation issues are permitted.

docs.title: CAD Model Import Guide
docs.text: fll-sim supports importing custom robot designs created in BrickLink Studio (.io) or LeoCAD / LDraw (.ldr, .mpd).

docs.title: 1. Importing BrickLink Studio (.io) Models
docs.text: BrickLink Studio is the most popular CAD tool used by FIRST LEGO League teams. Studio saves files in the .io format, which is an unencrypted ZIP archive containing: * model.ldr: The LDraw-formatted structural part hierarchy * thumbnail.png: Rendered thumbnail preview

docs.title: How to Import
docs.text:
1. In BrickLink Studio, save your robot model (File \(\to\) Save As... \(\to\) my_robot.io).
  2. Open the FLL Robot Simulator in your browser.
  3. In the top navigation bar, click 📂 Import Studio .io / .ldr.
  4. Select your .io file.
  5. The pre-solver will automatically:
  6. Unpack the model hierarchy
  7. Map part numbers to Technic physical mass and dimensions
  8. Cluster all static beams and pins
  9. Spawn your robot on the virtual competition table!

docs.title: 2. Importing LeoCAD / LDraw (.ldr, .mpd)
docs.text: If you use LeoCAD or the official LDraw library: 1. Export your model as .ldr (File \(\to\) Export \(\to\) LDraw...). 2. Upload the .ldr file through the 📂 Import button.

docs.title: 3. Modeling Best Practices for Simulation
docs.text: To ensure your CAD model clusters cleanly into the proper kinematic bodies: * Friction Pins vs. Axles: Use standard friction pins (2780, 6558) to connect beams rigidly to the chassis. * Motor Mounting: Ensure motor stators (45601, 45602) are rigidly pinned to the frame. * Wheel Axles: Ensure wheel rims (56145) are connected to motor output shafts with cross-axles. The clustering solver will automatically detect the 1-DOF rotational freedom and configure a revolute joint.

docs.title: SPIKE Prime Python API Reference
docs.text: fll-sim emulates the official LEGO SPIKE Prime Python API, allowing teams to test competition programs directly in the web browser.

docs.title: 1. PrimeHub & MotionSensor (Gyro)
docs.text:
from spike import PrimeHub

hub = PrimeHub()

# Reset Gyro heading to 0 degrees
hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()

# Read current yaw heading (-180 to +180 degrees)
yaw = hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle()
print("Current Yaw:", yaw)

docs.title: 2. MotorPair
docs.text:
from spike import MotorPair

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')

# Configure default speed (0 to 100%)
motors.set_default_speed(50)

# Move for specific distance or degrees
motors.move(30, 'cm')               # Drive 30 cm straight
motors.move(360, 'degrees')         # Move wheels 1 full rotation

# Steering move (steering: -100 hard left to +100 hard right)
motors.move(20, 'cm', steering=25)

# Tank move (independent left and right speeds)
motors.move_tank(180, 'degrees', left_speed=40, right_speed=-40)

# Continuous movement
motors.start(steering=0, speed=50)
motors.start_tank(30, 30)
motors.stop()

docs.title: 3. ColorSensor
docs.text:
from spike import ColorSensor

color_sensor = ColorSensor('C')

# Get reflected light intensity (0 to 100%)
# ~10-25% on black lines, ~80-100% on white mat
light = color_sensor.get_reflected_light()

# Get classified color name
# 'black', 'white', 'red', 'green', 'blue', 'yellow', 'none'
color_name = color_sensor.get_color()

docs.text:
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

# Non-blocking async sleep (yields execution to the physics engine)
wait_for_seconds(1.0)

docs.title: Mission 1: Straight Drive (30 cm)
docs.text:
from spike import MotorPair

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
motors.set_default_speed(50)
print("Driving 30 cm forward...")
motors.move(30, 'cm')
print("Done!")

docs.title: Mission 2: Gyro 90° Turn
docs.text:
from spike import PrimeHub, MotorPair
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

hub = PrimeHub()
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')

hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()
wait_for_seconds(0.2)

# Pivot turn until 90 degrees reached
motors.start_tank(35, -35)
while hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle() < 90:
    wait_for_seconds(0.01)

motors.stop()
print("Turn completed at yaw:", hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle())

docs.title: Mission 3: Proportional Line Follower (P-Controller)
docs.text:
from spike import MotorPair, ColorSensor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
color_c = ColorSensor('C')

target_light = 50   # Edge of line target (50% reflected light)
kp = 0.85           # Proportional gain
base_speed = 35     # Base driving velocity

for step in range(250):
    light = color_c.get_reflected_light()
    error = target_light - light
    steering = error * kp
    motors.start(steering, base_speed)
    wait_for_seconds(0.02)

motors.stop()
print("Line following sequence finished!")

docs.title: Mission 4: Dual-Sensor Line Squaring
docs.text:
from spike import MotorPair, ColorSensor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
sensor_c = ColorSensor('C') # Left
sensor_d = ColorSensor('D') # Right

# Drive toward line
motors.start(0, 30)
while sensor_c.get_reflected_light() > 30 and sensor_d.get_reflected_light() > 30:
    wait_for_seconds(0.01)
motors.stop()

# Align both sensors on the black line
for i in range(100):
    left_light = sensor_c.get_reflected_light()
    right_light = sensor_d.get_reflected_light()

    left_spd = 15 if left_light > 30 else 0
    right_spd = 15 if right_light > 30 else 0

    if left_spd == 0 and right_spd == 0:
        break

    motors.start_tank(left_spd, right_spd)
    wait_for_seconds(0.02)

motors.stop()
print("Robot perfectly squared to line!")

docs.title: 🧭 Welcome to the Virtual Competition Table
docs.text:
In traditional FLL robotics, teams face a familiar bottleneck: one 4x8 ft competition table, one SPIKE™ Prime robot hub, and 4 to 10 eager students waiting for their turn to test code.

fll-sim solves this challenge by delivering an open-source, 100% browser-based 3D robotics digital twin. Powered by Three.js WebGL rendering and Rapier 3D rigid-body physics running at 60 Hz, fll-sim emulates the exact kinematic behavior, sensor feedback, motor friction, and mission element interactions of an authentic competition table.

docs.title: How to Facilitate Team Sessions with fll-sim
docs.text:
1. Pair Programming Stations: Assign pairs of students (one "Driver" navigating the 3D viewport, one "Navigator" coding the mission blocks or Python). Switch roles every 15 minutes.
  2. Pre-Build Testing (The Digital Twin Strategy): Before building physical attachments out of Technic beams, have your CAD designers model them in BrickLink Studio. Load the .io file into Tutorial 5's CAD Inspector to verify center-of-mass, clearance, and lever arm mechanics.
  3. Reproducible Failure Analysis: When a run fails on the physical table, reproduce the starting angle and distance in the simulator. Is the failure caused by wheel slippage, gyro drift, or line detection sensitivity? The simulator's real-time telemetry dock pinpoints the exact cause in seconds.
  4. Engineering Notebook Evidence: Encourage students to capture screenshots of their telemetry plots, CAD clustering reports, and code blocks directly from fll-sim to paste into their team's FLL Engineering Notebook for the Robot Design judging session!

Hardware Requirements & System Compatibility

fll-sim runs entirely in client-side WebAssembly and WebGL:

  • Browsers: Google Chrome 90+, Mozilla Firefox 88+, Microsoft Edge 90+, Apple Safari 15+.
  • Operating Systems: ChromeOS, macOS, Windows 10/11, Ubuntu Linux.
  • Internet: Fully functional offline once loaded (all Draco 3D assets, LDraw geometry, and Python runtime are cached locally).
  • GPU: Integrated Intel/AMD graphics or dedicated GPUs (achieves consistent 60 FPS on standard classroom Chromebooks and laptops).

docs.title: 📖 Key FLL Robotics Terminology
docs.text:
Term Definition in FLL & fll-sim Launch Area (Red Arc / Home) The designated starting sector of the competition mat where the robot must fit completely within boundaries before launching autonomously. Starting Pose The precise initial position (X, Z) in meters and heading angle (Yaw °) of the robot chassis before ▶ RUN is triggered. Differential Drive A two-wheel drive system where steering is achieved by varying the relative rotational velocity of the left and right drive wheels. IMU / Gyro Yaw The internal 6-axis Inertial Measurement Unit inside the SPIKE Prime Hub tracking real-time angular heading in degrees (\(0^\circ \text{ to } 360^\circ\) or \(-180^\circ \text{ to } +180^\circ\)). Reflected Light Intensity An optical sensor measurement ranging from 0% (pitch black / matte tape) to 100% (pure white vinyl mat surface). Line Squaring An alignment routine using dual downward-facing optical sensors to straighten the robot perpendicularly against a field line. Topological Pin Clustering The simulator's algorithmic engine that groups 130+ Technic beams, pins, and axles into consolidated rigid bodies for high-speed 60 Hz physics.

Ready to begin? Head over to Tutorial 1: Navigating the 3D Mat & Your First Autonomous Run →!

docs.title: Tutorial 1: Navigating the 3D Mat & Your First Autonomous Run
docs.text: Welcome to your first hands-on session with the FLL Robot Simulator (fll-sim)! In this tutorial, you will explore the virtual 4x8 ft competition table, master camera navigation, launch your first autonomous robot run, inspect live sensor telemetry, and practice resetting the table with keyboard hotkeys.

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  1. Identify the official dimensions and key coordinate regions of the competition mat, including the Red Launch Arc.
  2. Seamlessly toggle between the Top-Down Programming Camera and the 3D Isometric View.
  3. Load and execute an autonomous Python mission using the simulator top bar.
  4. Read real-time telemetry from wheel motor encoders, optical color sensors, ultrasonic sonar, and the internal Gyro IMU.
  5. Instantaneously reset the robot to its exact starting pose using ↺ RESET and keyboard hotkeys.
  6. Complete Hands-On Challenge 1 by writing and verifying a calibrated autonomous drive routine.

docs.title: 🛠️ Step 1: Launching the Simulator and Understanding the 4x8 ft Competition Table
docs.text: When you open fll-sim in your browser (or run npm run dev locally), the complete 3D simulation environment renders in your browser window:

docs.title: The Anatomy of an FLL Competition Table
docs.text:
The competition table modeled in fll-sim matches the official FIRST® LEGO® League specifications:

  • Field Mat Dimensions: Standard 4x8 ft arena (approximately \(2.362\,\text{m} \times 1.143\,\text{m}\)).
  • Boundary Walls: Technic wooden perimeter borders with authentic collision friction and restitution.
  • Coordinate Grid:
    • The center of the mat is defined at X = 0.00 m, Z = 0.00 m.
    • X-Axis: Longitudinal axis along the length of the table (East/West direction).
    • Z-Axis: Transverse axis across the width of the table (North/South direction).
    • Y-Axis: Vertical height above the vinyl surface (Ground level = Y = 0.00 m).

Understanding Units in Robotics

In professional robotics and FLL competition rules, physical measurements are expressed in the Metric system. While the field table frame is colloquially referred to as "4x8 feet", all internal physics, sensor distances, and Python drive distances in fll-sim operate in centimeters (cm) and meters (m).

docs.title: 🚩 Step 2: The Red Launch Arc and Starting Pose
docs.text:
At the beginning of an official 2.5-minute FLL Robot Game match, your robot must begin completely inside one of the Launch Areas (the Red or Blue Home Arcs) on the edge of the mat.

In fll-sim, the default spawn pose positions the robot inside the Red Launch Arc:

  • Default Position: X = -0.80 m, Z = 0.32 m
  • Default Heading (Yaw): 90.0° (pointing directly East toward the field mission models)
  • Match Timer: Set to 02:30 (counts down dynamically during active runs)
flowchart TD
    A["🚩 Red Launch Arc
X: -0.80m, Z: 0.32m, Yaw: 90°"] -->|"Autonomous Run 1"| B["🔬 Field Mission Area
(Coral Reef / Bioglow Models)"]
    B -->|"Return to Home"| C["🏠 Home Base
(Attachment Swap & Reset)"]

You can view and modify the starting position anytime by clicking the ⚙️ Field button on the left activity bar. You can choose quick presets (🚩 Red Arc, 🔷 Blue Arc, or 🎯 Center), adjust the coordinates in millimeters, or rotate the heading by clicking ⟲ -45°, ⟳ +45°, or cardinal presets (0° N, 90° E, 180° S, 270° W). Once you have placed the robot in your desired spot, click 📌 Set as Start to lock it in!

docs.title: 🎥 Step 3: Top-Down Programming Camera vs. 3D Isometric View
docs.text:
Clear spatial perspective is crucial when debugging robot navigation. In the top bar, you have three dedicated camera presets:

[ 📐 3D Iso ]   [ 🗺️ Top-Down ]   [ 🎥 Follow ]

docs.title: 1. 🗺️ Top-Down (Programming & Navigation View)
docs.text:
• What it does: Positions an orthographic-style overhead camera looking straight down at the field mat.
  • When to use it: When designing line-following routes, measuring travel distances between mission models, and verifying that your robot drives in straight parallel lines without drifting.

docs.title: 2. 📐 3D Iso (Spatial & Attachment View)
docs.text:
• What it does: Positions a perspective camera at an elevated 45-degree angle with full 360-degree orbital controls.
  • Controls:
    • Left Click + Drag: Orbit / Rotate the table view.
    • Right Click + Drag: Pan horizontally and vertically across the mat.
    • Scroll Wheel: Smooth zoom in and out.
  • When to use it: When inspecting physical robot clearances, watching attachment levers lift or push mission models, or diagnosing wheel-wheel collision with field barriers.

docs.title: 3. 🎥 Follow (Driver's Chase Cam)
docs.text: • What it does: Locks the camera directly behind the robot's rear chassis, dynamically tracking the robot as it turns and accelerates across the mat.

docs.title: ▶️ Step 4: Selecting and Running Sample Mission 1 ("Drive Straight 30 cm")
docs.text:
Let's execute your first autonomous run!

Look at the Top Navigation Bar at the upper-right corner of your screen:

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution:
docs.text:
1. Select Mission: In the 📜 Program dropdown menu, ensure Mission 1: Drive Straight (30 cm) is selected.
  2. Review Code: Click 💻 Code Editor in the top bar to inspect the Python code that will run: 
    from spike import MotorPair

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
motors.set_default_speed(50)

print("Driving 30 cm forward...")
motors.move(30, 'cm')
print("Done!")
  3. Execute Run: Click the bright green ▶ RUN button.
  4. Watch the Simulation:
    • The match countdown timer begins ticking (02:29, 02:28...).
    • The virtual motors on Ports A and B smoothly accelerate to 50% power.
    • The robot moves forward along the mat by exactly 30 centimeters (\(0.30\,\text{m}\)).
    • The console output prints Driving 30 cm forward... followed by Done!.
    • The top bar switches back from ⏹ STOP to ▶ RUN.

docs.title: 📡 Step 5: Reading Real-Time Telemetry
docs.text:
While the robot moves, how do we know exactly what its motors and sensors are doing? Click the 📡 Telemetry button in the top bar to open the Live Telemetry & Diagnostics Dock:

The Telemetry Dock is divided into three comprehensive diagnostic tabs:

docs.title: 1. Optical & Environmental Sensors (📡 Sensors & Pose)
docs.text:
• Color Sensor C (Left) & Color Sensor D (Right): Displays current Reflected Light Intensity (\(0\% \text{ to } 100\%\)) and the classified surface color (WHITE, BLACK, RED, GREEN, BLUE). When driving over white vinyl, reflected light reads \(85\% \text{ to } 95\%\). When passing over black navigation lines, it drops to \(15\% \text{ to } 22\%\).
  • Ultrasonic Distance Sensor: Measures sonar distance to the nearest barrier or mission model (\(0 \text{ to } 150\,\text{cm}\)).
  • Internal 6-Axis Gyro IMU: Displays real-time heading yaw with an interactive compass needle dial. Heading increases clockwise (\(0.0^\circ \text{ to } 360.0^\circ\)).
  • Robot Field Coordinates: Live \((X, Z)\) coordinate readouts and global orientation yaw.

docs.title: 2. Motor Encoders & Speeds (⚙️ Motors)
docs.text:
• Drive Motors A & B: Shows accumulated rotational angle in degrees (\(^\circ\)), instantaneous angular velocity (\(\text{deg/s}\)), and calculated linear travel distance (\(\text{cm}\)).
  • Auxiliary Motors C–F: Displays state, target angles, and load for attachment arms.
  • Control Actions: Includes quick-access buttons for ⏹ Stop All Motors and ↺ Zero Encoders.

docs.title: 3. Live Command & Event Logs (telem-dock-right)
docs.text: • A real-time chronological stream of every API instruction executed by the robot (MOTOR_RUN, STEER, BRAKE_HOLD, SENSOR_POLL). You can filter entries by clicking Drive, Brake, or Motors, or clear history with 🧹 Clear Logs.

docs.title: ↺ Step 6: Resetting the Robot with ↺ RESET and Ctrl+Space
docs.text: In competition development, you will test, adjust, and re-test hundreds of times. Fast resetting is essential for efficient workflow.

docs.title: Two Ways to Instantaneously Reset:
docs.text:
1. Top Bar Button: Click the yellow ↺ RESET button in the top navigation bar.
  2. Keyboard Hotkey: Press Ctrl + Space (or Cmd + Space on macOS) anywhere in the application.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle: Robot in Red Arc
    Idle --> Running: Click ▶ RUN
    Running --> Finished: Mission Completes
    Running --> Interrupted: Click ⏹ STOP
    Finished --> Idle: Click ↺ RESET or Ctrl+Space
    Interrupted --> Idle: Click ↺ RESET or Ctrl+Space

docs.title: What Happens During a Reset?
docs.text:
• The robot chassis snaps back to its starting spawn position (X = -0.80 m, Z = 0.32 m).
  • The heading yaw returns to its calibrated starting orientation (90.0°).
  • All linear and angular momentum in the Rapier 3D physics engine is zeroed.
  • Motor encoders on Ports A and B are zeroed to \(0^\circ\).
  • The Gyro IMU yaw angle is recalibrated to \(0.0^\circ\).
  • The Python execution runtime is reset to the IDLE state.

docs.title: 🏆 Hands-On Challenge 1: The 50 cm Calibration Run
docs.text: Now it's time to test your skills!

docs.title: Challenge Prompt:
docs.text:
Goal: Your team needs to drive from the Red Launch Arc past the first set of field navigation lines, stopping precisely at \(50.0\,\text{cm}\) (\(0.50\,\text{m}\)) from your start point.

Requirements: 1. Set the robot's starting position in the Red Arc facing East (\(90^\circ\)). 2. Open the Code Editor and create a new script named challenge_1_calibration.py. 3. Program the robot to drive forward for \(50.0\,\text{cm}\) at \(40\%\) speed. 4. Verify in the Telemetry Dock that the distance traveled reads between \(49.5\,\text{cm}\) and \(50.5\,\text{cm}\). 5. Print a message to the console reporting the final Gyro Yaw heading to confirm that the robot drove straight without yaw drift.

docs.title: Challenge 1 Solution
docs.text:
Python SolutionWord Blocks Solution 
from spike import PrimeHub, MotorPair
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

# 1. Initialize the Hub and Drive Motor Pair
hub = PrimeHub()
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')

# 2. Reset sensors for a clean test
hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()
wait_for_seconds(0.2)

print("--- CHALLENGE 1: 50 CM CALIBRATION RUN ---")
print("Initial Yaw:", hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle())

# 3. Configure speed for high odometry accuracy (40%)
motors.set_default_speed(40)

# 4. Execute the 50 cm drive
motors.move(50, 'cm')

# 5. Read final Gyro yaw to detect any wheel slip drift
final_yaw = hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle()
print("Drive complete!")
print("Final Heading Yaw:", final_yaw, "degrees")

if abs(final_yaw) < 1.0:
    print("✅ SUCCESS: Perfectly straight run with less than 1° drift!")
else:
    print("⚠️ NOTE: Heading drifted by", final_yaw, "degrees.")

docs.title: Why Does Speed Matter for Calibration?
docs.text: When differential drive robots travel at \(100\%\) maximum velocity, the rapid initial acceleration can cause microscopic wheel slip against the vinyl mat. By reducing your default speed to \(35\% \text{--} 50\%\), the tire rubber maintains maximum static friction, resulting in highly repeatable autonomous runs on both the simulator and your real table!

docs.title: ⏭️ Next Step
docs.text: Now that you've mastered 3D mat navigation and the execution workflow, continue to Tutorial 2: Programming with LEGO SPIKE Prime Word Blocks → to learn how to build complex missions using visual Scratch-based blocks!

docs.title: Tutorial 2: Programming with LEGO SPIKE Prime Word Blocks
docs.text:
For many FIRST LEGO League teams, the official LEGO® SPIKE™ Prime Word Blocks environment is the go-to programming language. Based on Google Blockly and Scratch 3.0, Word Blocks provides an intuitive, color-coded drag-and-drop interface that makes autonomous robotics accessible to students of all skill levels.

In this tutorial, you will explore the simulator's built-in Word Blocks Studio, build a multi-step autonomous drive and attachment mission, learn how to manage and zoom your block canvas, and export/import competition files.

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  1. Open and arrange the Word Blocks Studio in both the Collapsible Side Drawer and the Full-Screen Popout Modal.
  2. Navigate the 3-Column SPIKE Workspace (Category Sidebar, Block Palette Drawer, and Dotted Canvas).
  3. Assemble a complete 6-block autonomous mission controlling both drive motors and an auxiliary attachment motor.
  4. Pan, zoom, and organize multi-step block stacks on the canvas.
  5. Save your work with built-in Autosave, export projects as .zip bundles, and import official LEGO .llsp3 project files.
  6. Solve Hands-On Challenge 2 by creating a simulated Coral Reef mission run.

docs.title: 🖥️ Step 1: Opening the Word Blocks Studio (Drawer vs. Popout Modal)
docs.text: fll-sim offers two flexible ways to work with Word Blocks:

docs.title: 1. The Collapsible Side Drawer View
docs.text:
Click the 💻 Code button on the far-left Activity Bar. The side drawer expands on the left, displaying your block stack right alongside the 3D competition table:

  • Best For: Rapid tweaking and quick testing where you want to watch the robot drive in the 3D viewport while seeing the active block highlights.

docs.title: 2. The Full-Screen Popout Modal
docs.text:
When building complex, multi-step programs with dozens of blocks, you need maximum screen real estate. Click either: * The 💻 Code Editor button in the top navigation bar, OR * The ⤢ Pop Out button located in the drawer header.

  • Window Pinning Controls (Top Right of Modal):
    • ⛶ Maximize (Full-Screen): Expands the Studio across your entire monitor.
    • ◧ Pin Left: Snaps the block canvas to the left half of the screen, leaving the right half open for the 3D field.
    • ◨ Pin Right: Snaps the block canvas to the right half of the screen.
    • 🗗 Float: Turns the editor into a draggable, resizable floating window.
    • ⤓ Dock Back: Collapses the modal back into the side drawer.

docs.title: 1. Category Sidebar (Far Left)
docs.text: Color-coded icons that filter available blocks by functional robotics subsystem: * Motors (Blue): Single-motor commands for attachments on Ports C, D, E, and F (run for degrees, seconds, speed). * Movement (Pink): Synchronized differential drive base commands for Ports A+B (move forward, backward, tank turns, steering). * Events (Yellow): Program initiation triggers (when program starts, broadcast messages). * Control (Orange): Execution flow (wait 1 seconds, repeat 10, forever, if...then...else). * Sensors (Cyan): Optical color sensor, ultrasonic distance, and Hub IMU gyro readings. * Operators (Green): Mathematical math blocks (\(+\), \(-\), \(\times\), \(\div\), comparisons, random numbers).

docs.title: 2. Block Palette Drawer (Center)
docs.text: Displays the library of available blocks for the selected category. You can drag any block from this drawer directly into your canvas.

docs.title: 3. Canvas Viewport (Right)
docs.text: An infinite dotted-grid workspace where you assemble your code. Blocks automatically snap together with an audible and visual click when brought close to a compatible connector notch.

docs.title: 🚀 Step 3: Creating a Precision Drive & Attachment Mission
docs.text:
Let's build a competition mission that drives our robot forward out of the Red Arc, activates an attachment mechanism to interact with a mission model, and then backs up safely to Home Base.

flowchart TD
    Start["🟡 when program starts"] --> Motors["🌸 set movement motors to A+B"]
    Motors --> Speed["🌸 set movement speed to 50%"]
    Speed --> DriveOut["🌸 move forward for 35 cm"]
    DriveOut --> Lever["🔵 motor E run clockwise for 90 degrees"]
    Lever --> Return["🌸 move backward for 35 cm"]

docs.title: Assemble the 6 Core Blocks:
docs.text:
1. when program starts (Events - Yellow):
    • Every FLL program begins with this hat block. It acts as the execution entry point when you press ▶ RUN.
  2. set movement motors to [A + B] (Movement - Pink):
    • Tells the virtual SPIKE Hub which motor ports drive the left and right wheels. By default, the Advanced Driving Base uses Port A for the left wheel and Port B for the right wheel.
  3. set movement speed to [50] % (Movement - Pink):
    • Configures the cruising velocity. Running at \(50\%\) provides the optimal balance of speed and mechanical stability on the competition mat.
  4. move [forward] for [35] [cm] (Movement - Pink):
    • The simulator's kinematic model calculates the exact rotational degrees needed for the 56 mm rubber wheels to travel 35 cm: $\(\text{Rotations} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\pi \times \text{Diameter}} = \frac{35\,\text{cm}}{\pi \times 5.6\,\text{cm}} \approx 1.989\,\text{rotations} \approx 716^\circ\)$
  5. motor [E] run [clockwise] for [90] [degrees] (Motors - Blue):
    • Activates the auxiliary motor connected to Port E. This turns your attachment lever by exactly a quarter rotation (\(90^\circ\)), lifting or pressing the mission model.
  6. move [backward] for [35] [cm] (Movement - Pink):
    • Reverses the drive motors, bringing your robot back behind the Home Arc perimeter line.

docs.title: Running the Mission:
docs.text:
1. Click ▶ RUN at the bottom of the editor (or in the top bar).
  2. Watch the 3D viewport:
    • The robot accelerates smoothly out of the Red Arc.
    • At 35 cm, the drive motors brake.
    • Motor E rotates its output shaft by \(90^\circ\).
    • The robot reverses 35 cm directly back to the starting line!

docs.title: 🔍 Step 4: Zooming and Organizing Canvas Blocks
docs.text:
As your team develops multiple runs for different missions, your canvas will grow. fll-sim includes full pan and zoom navigation:

  • Mouse Wheel: Scroll up to zoom in, scroll down to zoom out.
  • Canvas Panning: Click and drag any empty area of the dotted canvas background to pan smoothly across your workspace.
  • Floating Zoom Controls (Bottom-Right of Canvas):
    • ➕ Button: Zooms in by \(15\%\).
    • ➖ Button: Zooms out by \(15\%\).
    • ↺ 100% Button: Instantly resets magnification to \(100\%\) and centers the active block stack.
    • Zoom Badge: Displays current magnification (\(50\% \text{ to } 200\%\)).

Judging Tip: Clean Canvas & Code Comments

FLL Robot Design judges love clean code! Keep separate mission runs organized in clear columns across your canvas. Right-click any block to add an explanatory comment (e.g., "Mission 1: Coral Reef push and lever release"). Judges will award high marks for well-documented software engineering!

docs.title: 💾 Step 5: Autosave, Exporting Scripts, and Importing .llsp3 Files
docs.text: Never lose team progress! The simulator includes a multi-tier persistence engine:

docs.title: 1. Instant Autosave
docs.text: Notice the 💾 Saved green status indicator in the editor toolbar. Every change you make—dragging a block, editing a parameter value, or creating a new tab—is immediately saved to your browser's persistent local storage. If you accidentally close your browser tab, your complete program will be restored the moment you return!

docs.title: 2. Exporting Single Scripts and ZIP Archives
docs.text:
• 💾 Export: Downloads the currently active script as a standalone .py Python file.
  • 📦 Export Zip: Bundles all active scripts, word blocks configurations, and custom missions into a single timestamped .zip archive.
    • Coach Recommended Workflow: Have your team's software lead click 📦 Export Zip at the end of every team meeting and upload the archive to Google Drive or GitHub.

docs.title: 3. Importing Existing Team Files
docs.text:
Click 📥 Import Code to upload: * Official LEGO SPIKE App v3 projects (.llsp3) * Legacy SPIKE App v2 projects (.llsp) * Scratch 3.0 projects (.sb3) * Standard Python scripts (.py)

The simulator's built-in spike-scratch-importer parses the JSON AST inside the .llsp3 ZIP container and instantly recreates the visual blocks on your canvas!

docs.title: 🏆 Hands-On Challenge 2: The Coral Reef Lift & Return Mission
docs.text: Put your Word Blocks skills into practice with a realistic season challenge!

docs.title: Challenge Prompt:
docs.text:
Scenario: The robot must leave the Red Launch Arc, navigate \(42.0\,\text{cm}\) across the field, stop in front of the coral nursery, lower an attachment arm on Port E by \(120^\circ\) to hook the coral branch, wait \(0.5\) seconds for physics stabilization, lift the coral branch by \(120^\circ\) counter-clockwise, and finally drive backward \(42.0\,\text{cm}\) into Home Base.

Requirements: 1. Set movement speed to \(45\%\). 2. Ensure motor E stops with brake mode enabled. 3. Use an orange wait block between lowering and lifting to allow physical contact settling. 4. Verify in the Telemetry Dock that the robot returns within \(0.5\,\text{cm}\) of the start line.

docs.title: Challenge 2 Solution
docs.text:
Word Blocks StackGenerated SPIKE Python Equivalent 
[when program starts]
[set movement motors to A+B]
[set movement speed to 45%]
[move forward for 42 cm]
[motor E set stop action to [hold]]
[motor E run clockwise for 120 degrees]
[wait 0.5 seconds]
[motor E run counterclockwise for 120 degrees]
[move backward for 42 cm]
[stop [all motors]]

from spike import MotorPair, Motor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

# Initialize Drive Base and Attachment Motor E
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
motor_e = Motor('E')

# Configure cruising speed
motors.set_default_speed(45)

print("Step 1: Driving 42 cm to Coral Reef...")
motors.move(42, 'cm')

print("Step 2: Lowering attachment arm 120 degrees...")
motor_e.run_for_degrees(120, speed=30)

# Allow Rapier 3D physics settling
wait_for_seconds(0.5)

print("Step 3: Lifting coral branch 120 degrees...")
motor_e.run_for_degrees(-120, speed=30)

print("Step 4: Returning to Home Base...")
motors.move(-42, 'cm')

print("Mission Complete!")

docs.title: Why Include a 0.5-Second Wait Block?
docs.text: In physical robotics, momentum and elastic rebound occur when Technic beams impact plastic mission elements. Pausing for \(0.5\) seconds lets vibrations dissipate and allows the attachment teeth to seat securely before reversing direction. This simple habit prevents dropped mission elements on the competition field!

docs.title: Tutorial 3: Authentic SPIKE Python Programming & Autonomous Navigation
docs.text:
While visual Word Blocks are fantastic for getting started, text-based Python provides the ultimate speed, algorithmic precision, and mathematical control for high-scoring FIRST® LEGO® League competition teams.

In this tutorial, you will write authentic Python scripts using the official spike library syntax, implement closed-loop Gyro IMU pivot turns, design a smooth Proportional (P-Controller) Line Follower, build an error-eliminating Dual-Sensor Line Squaring routine, and debug issues using the simulator's Live Event Log Stream.

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  1. Import and instantiate PrimeHub, MotorPair, ColorSensor, and control timers from the spike library.
  2. Replace inconsistent dead-reckoning wheel turns with closed-loop Gyro 90° Precision Tank Turns.
  3. Understand the mathematics of a Proportional (P) Controller to track the boundary of field lines without oscillating.
  4. Program a Dual-Sensor Line Squaring algorithm that realigns the robot's heading to zero-drift precision.
  5. Inspect the Live Command & Event Logs stream to diagnose motor latency, sensor polling rates, and physics collisions.
  6. Solve Hands-On Challenge 3 by programming a multi-stage autonomous navigation routine.

docs.title: 🐍 Step 1: Writing Python for the Virtual SPIKE Prime Hub
docs.text:
In fll-sim, the Python environment runs directly in your browser using an asynchronous Python-to-TypeScript runtime that faithfully implements the official LEGO SPIKE Prime Python API.

To switch to Python mode: 1. Open the Code Editor (either in the side drawer or popout modal). 2. Click the 💻 Python toggle button in the header bar. 3. You now have a full-featured code editor with syntax highlighting and auto-indentation.

docs.title: The Essential SPIKE Library Imports
docs.text:
Every competition script typically begins with these core imports:

from spike import PrimeHub, MotorPair, ColorSensor, Motor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

# Initialize the Hub (provides access to the 6-axis Gyro IMU)
hub = PrimeHub()

# Initialize differential drive motors on Ports A and B
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')

# Initialize optical color sensors on Ports C (Left) and D (Right)
color_left = ColorSensor('C')
color_right = ColorSensor('D')

Crucial Concept: wait_for_seconds() in Simulation

In physical MicroPython on the SPIKE Hub, a time.sleep() halts the processor core. In a browser simulation, however, calling blocking sleeps freezes the WebGL render loop!

Always use from spike.control import wait_for_seconds. The simulator's wait_for_seconds() yields execution cooperatively back to the browser, allowing the Rapier 3D physics engine and Three.js canvas to step forward at a rock-solid 60 FPS while your loop runs.

docs.title: Why Do "Turn for Degrees" Moves Fail in FLL?
docs.text:
Many rookie teams program turns by running one wheel forward for \(180^\circ\) and the other backward for \(180^\circ\). While this works on clean paper, it constantly drifts on competition mats due to: * Dust and static friction differences on vinyl surfaces. * Varying battery voltage (a low battery turns slower than a fresh battery). * Center-of-mass shifts from heavy attachment arms.

The professional solution is closed-loop feedback using the Hub's internal 6-axis Gyroscope!

flowchart TD
    A["Reset Gyro Yaw to 0.0°"] --> B["Start Counter-Rotating Motors\nLeft: +35%, Right: -35%"]
    B --> C{"Is Gyro Yaw >= 90.0°?"}
    C -- No --> D["wait_for_seconds(0.01)\nPoll Sensor"]
    D --> C
    C -- Yes --> E["Brake Motors\nmotors.stop()"]
    E --> F["Turn Complete at 90°!"]

docs.title: Gyro Turn Implementation:
docs.text:
from spike import PrimeHub, MotorPair
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

hub = PrimeHub()
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')

# 1. Reset Gyro Yaw heading to zero
hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()
wait_for_seconds(0.2)  # Brief pause for IMU baseline settling

print("Starting Gyro 90° Pivot Turn...")

# 2. Start a tank pivot (Left wheel forward, Right wheel backward)
motors.start_tank(35, -35)

# 3. Closed-loop monitoring: keep turning until 90 degrees reached
while hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle() < 90:
    wait_for_seconds(0.01)

# 4. Instant active braking
motors.stop()

final_yaw = hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle()
print(f"Turn successfully locked in at Yaw: {final_yaw:.1f}°")

docs.title: Key Parameters:
docs.text:
• start_tank(35, -35): Turning at \(35\%\) speed ensures the robot doesn't overshoot \(90^\circ\) due to rotational inertia.
  • get_yaw_angle(): Returns the instantaneous angular orientation relative to the last zero point.
  • wait_for_seconds(0.01): High-frequency 100 Hz sensor polling loop.

docs.title: 〰️ Step 3: Proportional Line Follower (P-Controller)
docs.text:
On an FLL field, black guide lines link your launch sector directly to key mission models. Simple "two-state" (bang-bang) line followers oscillate violently back and forth like a snake.

A Proportional (P) Controller calculates the mathematical error between where the robot is and where it wants to be, smoothly adjusting steering proportionally to that error.

flowchart LR
    Target["Target Light\n50% (Line Edge)"] --> Diff["Calculate Error:\nError = Target - Light"]
    Sensor["ColorSensor('C')\nLight Reading"] --> Diff
    Diff --> Gain["Multiply Gain:\nSteering = Error * Kp"]
    Gain --> Drive["motors.start(steering, speed)"]

docs.title: The Mathematics:
docs.text:
1. Target: We follow the edge where white vinyl (\(90\%\) light) meets black line (\(20\%\) light). The target is the midpoint: $\(\text{Target} = 50\%\)$
  2. Error: The difference between our target and what Color Sensor C currently sees: $\(\text{Error} = \text{Target} - \text{Reflected Light}\)$
  3. Steering Correction: $\(\text{Steering} = \text{Error} \times K_p\)$ where \(K_p\) is the Proportional Gain (typically \(0.7 \text{ to } 1.0\)).

docs.title: Proportional Line Follower Implementation:
docs.text:
from spike import MotorPair, ColorSensor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
color_c = ColorSensor('C')  # Left downward optical sensor

TARGET_LIGHT = 50   # 50% reflected light = edge of black line
KP = 0.85           # Proportional tuning constant
CRUISE_SPEED = 35   # Stable driving speed

print("Engaging Proportional Line Tracking...")

# Run line follower for 250 control cycles (approx. 5 seconds)
for cycle in range(250):
    current_light = color_c.get_reflected_light()

    # Calculate error and steering adjustment
    error = TARGET_LIGHT - current_light
    steering = error * KP

    # Apply steering correction with forward velocity
    motors.start(steering=int(steering), speed=CRUISE_SPEED)
    wait_for_seconds(0.02)  # 50 Hz control loop

motors.stop()
print("Line tracking complete!")

Tuning Proportional Gain (\(K_p\))

  • If \(K_p\) is too low (\(< 0.4\)): The robot responds too sluggishly and drifts off sharp line curves.
  • If \(K_p\) is too high (\(> 1.5\)): The robot jerks and oscillates violently.
  • For the Advanced Driving Base in fll-sim, a \(K_p\) between \(0.75\) and \(0.90\) provides glass-smooth tracking!

docs.title: 📐 Step 4: Dual-Sensor Line Squaring Algorithm
docs.text:
In high-level FLL competition, teams cannot rely on odometry alone across a long 2.5-minute run. Small tire slips accumulate into large positional errors.

The Dual-Sensor Line Squaring routine is the gold standard for resetting positional and angular error: as the robot approaches a black perpendicular line, each wheel moves independently until both downward sensors detect black. The robot is then mathematically guaranteed to be square (\(90.0^\circ\)) to the line!

sequenceDiagram
    participant Robot as Chassis (Motors A & B)
    participant SensC as Sensor C (Left)
    participant SensD as Sensor D (Right)
    participant Mat as Black Field Line

    Note over Robot,Mat: Phase 1: Drive forward toward line
    Robot->>Mat: Driving at 30% speed
    SensC-->>Robot: Sees White (85%)
    SensD-->>Robot: Sees White (85%)
    SensC->>Mat: Hits Black Line (20%)!
    Robot->>Robot: Stop forward movement!

    Note over Robot,Mat: Phase 2: Independent wheel creeping
    loop Until Both on Black Line
        alt Left Sensor still on White?
            Robot->>Robot: Creep Left Wheel (A) at 15%
        else Left Sensor on Black?
            Robot->>Robot: Brake Left Wheel (A) at 0%
        end
        alt Right Sensor still on White?
            Robot->>Robot: Creep Right Wheel (B) at 15%
        else Right Sensor on Black?
            Robot->>Robot: Brake Right Wheel (B) at 0%
        end
    end
    Note over Robot,Mat: Robot is now 100% Squared!

docs.title: Line Squaring Implementation:
docs.text:
from spike import MotorPair, ColorSensor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
sensor_c = ColorSensor('C')  # Left sensor
sensor_d = ColorSensor('D')  # Right sensor

BLACK_THRESHOLD = 30  # Light < 30% indicates black tape

print("Phase 1: Driving toward black line...")
motors.start(steering=0, speed=30)

# Drive forward until EITHER sensor detects the line
while sensor_c.get_reflected_light() > BLACK_THRESHOLD and sensor_d.get_reflected_light() > BLACK_THRESHOLD:
    wait_for_seconds(0.01)

motors.stop()
print("Line detected! Phase 2: Squaring heading...")

# Align both wheels until BOTH sensors rest precisely on black
for step in range(120):
    left_light = sensor_c.get_reflected_light()
    right_light = sensor_d.get_reflected_light()

    # Move each wheel only if its sensor hasn't reached black yet
    left_speed = 15 if left_light > BLACK_THRESHOLD else 0
    right_speed = 15 if right_light > BLACK_THRESHOLD else 0

    # If both wheels have reached the black line, we are perfectly square!
    if left_speed == 0 and right_speed == 0:
        print("Both sensors locked on black line!")
        break

    motors.start_tank(left_speed, right_speed)
    wait_for_seconds(0.02)

motors.stop()
print("Robot perfectly squared to field line!")

docs.title: 🏆 Hands-On Challenge 3: Turn, Track & Square Sequence
docs.text: Combine all three autonomous techniques into a single, tournament-grade navigation routine!

docs.title: Challenge Prompt:
docs.text: Mission Scenario: 1. Start inside the Red Launch Arc facing East (\(90^\circ\)). 2. Execute a precision Gyro Pivot Turn \(45^\circ\) to the left to align with the diagonal field line (Target Yaw = \(45.0^\circ\)). 3. Drive forward using the Proportional Line Follower for \(3.0\) seconds along the line edge. 4. Disengage line following and perform a Dual-Sensor Line Squaring maneuver against the cross-line. 5. Print a final diagnostic report confirming that both sensors read black and reporting the calibrated Gyro heading.

docs.title: Challenge 3 Solution
docs.text:
from spike import PrimeHub, MotorPair, ColorSensor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

# 1. Hardware Initialization
hub = PrimeHub()
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')
color_left = ColorSensor('C')
color_right = ColorSensor('D')

# Calibrate Gyro
hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()
wait_for_seconds(0.2)
print("=== MISSION RUN: TURN, TRACK & SQUARE ===")

# STEP 1: Precision Gyro Turn to 45 degrees
print("Step 1: Pivot turning to 45 degrees...")
motors.start_tank(-30, 30)  # Counter-clockwise pivot
while hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle() > -45:
    wait_for_seconds(0.01)
motors.stop()
print(f"Turn complete. Current Yaw: {hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle():.1f}°")

# STEP 2: Proportional Line Follower on Color Sensor C
print("Step 2: Tracking line for 3 seconds...")
TARGET_LIGHT = 50
KP = 0.8
CRUISE_SPEED = 35

for step in range(150):  # 150 cycles * 0.02s = 3.0 seconds
    light = color_left.get_reflected_light()
    error = TARGET_LIGHT - light
    steering = int(error * KP)
    motors.start(steering, CRUISE_SPEED)
    wait_for_seconds(0.02)

motors.stop()
print("Step 2 complete.")

# STEP 3: Dual-Sensor Line Squaring
print("Step 3: Squaring against cross-line...")
motors.start(0, 25)
while color_left.get_reflected_light() > 30 and color_right.get_reflected_light() > 30:
    wait_for_seconds(0.01)
motors.stop()

# Fine adjustment loop
for i in range(100):
    l_light = color_left.get_reflected_light()
    r_light = color_right.get_reflected_light()

    l_spd = 12 if l_light > 30 else 0
    r_spd = 12 if r_light > 30 else 0

    if l_spd == 0 and r_spd == 0:
        break

    motors.start_tank(l_spd, r_spd)
    wait_for_seconds(0.02)

motors.stop()

# STEP 4: Final Telemetry Verification
print("=== SEQUENCE COMPLETE ===")
print(f"Left Sensor (Port C): {color_left.get_reflected_light()}% [Black: {color_left.get_color()}]")
print(f"Right Sensor (Port D): {color_right.get_reflected_light()}% [Black: {color_right.get_color()}]")
print(f"Final Calibrated Yaw: {hub.motion_sensor.get_yaw_angle():.1f}°")
print("Robot is ready for attachment trigger!")

docs.title: Tutorial 4: Robot Architecture, Hardware Port Mapping & Calibration
docs.text:
In FIRST LEGO League, no two team robots are built identically. Your team might build the official WRO/FLL DroidBot-E, design a nimble Compact SPIKE Base, or place your drive motors on Ports E and F instead of Ports A and B.

To make the simulator a true Digital Twin of your physical robot, fll-sim includes a dynamic Robot Design & Hardware Port Inspector. In this tutorial, you will explore built-in chassis presets, remap hardware ports to mirror your real-world robot, test mechanisms safely in Dyno Jig Mode, and master encoder and gyro calibration.

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  1. Compare the mechanical kinematics of the Advanced Driving Base (DroidBot-E) and the Compact SPIKE Base.
  2. Navigate the Hardware Device Matrix for drive motors, auxiliary attachments, optical sensors, sonar, and the internal IMU.
  3. Dynamically remap Hub Ports A through F to match your physical team robot without changing your code.
  4. Engage Dyno Jig Mode to benchmark and test attachment mechanisms while the chassis remains anchored stationary.
  5. Zero motor encoders and calibrate Gyro IMU heading for reproducible competition runs.
  6. Complete Hands-On Challenge 4 by configuring a non-standard port layout and verifying an attachment cycle in Dyno mode.

docs.title: 🏎️ Step 1: Exploring Robot Presets (Advanced Driving Base vs. Compact Base)
docs.text:
To open the hardware inspector, click 🤖 Robot Design in the top navigation bar:

Under SECTION A: Robot Architecture & CAD Model Selection, you will see two official competition chassis presets:

docs.title: 1. Advanced Driving Base (DroidBot-E)
docs.text:
• Design Background: Based on the world-renowned DroidBot-E / LEGO Education competition reference architecture.
  • Chassis Specifications:
    • Track Width (\(W\)): \(128\,\text{mm}\) (16 Technic studs between left and right wheel centers).
    • Wheels: \(56\,\text{mm} \times 26\,\text{mm}\) balloon rubber tires (Circumference \(\approx 17.59\,\text{cm}\)).
    • Rear Caster: Steel ball caster housing with ultra-low rolling friction (\(\mu = 0.005\)).
    • Sensors: Dual downward-facing Color Sensors (Ports C & D) spaced 48 mm apart, plus forward Ultrasonic Sonar (Port E).
    • Total Mass: \(475\,\text{g}\) with a realistic low center of mass (\(Y = 32\,\text{mm}\) above the table).
  • Best For: Multi-mission runs requiring dual-line squaring, push attachments, and heavy payload stability.

docs.title: 2. Compact SPIKE Base
docs.text:
• Design Background: Minimalist, high-agility differential drive chassis.
  • Chassis Specifications:
    • Track Width (\(W\)): \(112\,\text{mm}\) (14 Technic studs).
    • Wheels: \(56\,\text{mm}\) slim rubber tires.
    • Mass: \(340\,\text{g}\) (nearly \(30\%\) lighter than the Advanced base).
  • Best For: High-speed sprint missions, agile zero-radius spin turns, and tight navigation between crowded mission models.

To switch active robots, click the preset card. The simulator's 3D engine immediately hot-swaps the kinematic physics model and visual mesh on the field!

docs.title: 🔄 Step 3: Remapping Ports to Match Your Team's Robot
The Problem in Real FLL Practice:
docs.text:
Your team built a custom robot. Because of cable routing constraints, the builders plugged: * Drive motors into Ports E & F (instead of A & B). * Attachment motors into Ports A & B. * Color sensors into Ports C & D.

In many simulators, you would have to rewrite all your code. In fll-sim, you simply remap the virtual hardware!

docs.title: How to Remap Ports:
docs.text:
1. In the Robot Design & Hardware Port Inspector, locate the component card you want to adjust (e.g., Drive Left Wheel).
  2. Open the Assigned Port dropdown and select the new port letter (e.g., change Port A to Port E).
  3. Repeat for other components until your virtual setup matches your physical robot.
  4. Click the blue 💾 Save Port Mapping button in the modal footer.

docs.title: 🔒 Step 4: Dyno Jig Mode (Stationary Mechanism Testing)
docs.text:
In physical robotics engineering, a Dynamometer (Dyno) or test bench anchors a vehicle stationary while its powertrain, transmissions, and mechanisms are tested at full throttle.

In fll-sim, Dyno Jig Mode anchors the robot chassis to the mat with a rigid physics pin, while allowing all drive wheels, motors, and attachment arms to spin freely under full simulated power!

│ 🔒 DYNO JIG ACTIVE: Chassis Locked | Actuators Live         │
│                                                             │
│         [Drive Wheels Spin]       [Attachment Arms Sweep]   │
│                 ↺                           ⟳               │
│               ┌───┐                       ┌───┐             │
│               │ A │                       │ E │             │
│            ┌──┴───┴───────────────────────┴───┴──┐          │
│            │   ⚓ ANCHORED CHASSIS (X, Z Fixed)   │          │

docs.title: Why Use Dyno Jig Mode?
docs.text:
1. Attachment Range of Motion: Verify that your motorized arm rotates exactly \(90^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\) without having the robot drive across the field.
  2. Gear Backlash & Timing: Measure the real time (in milliseconds) required for a rack-and-pinion attachment to extend and retract.
  3. Desk Testing Without Field Space: Test your Python logic while keeping the robot in the exact same spot on the virtual table.

docs.title: How to Activate Dyno Jig:
docs.text:
1. Open the ⚙️ Field drawer on the left activity bar.
  2. Under Sandbox Workbench Tools, click 🔒 Robot Dyno: OFF.
  3. The button label changes to 🟢 Robot Dyno: ACTIVE and a status banner appears.
  4. Run your code! Watch the motors turn in the Telemetry Dock while the coordinates (X, Z) remain perfectly stationary.
  5. Click the button again to release the anchor when you are ready to test driving.

docs.title: 🧭 Step 5: Zeroing Encoders and Calibrating Gyro IMU Heading
docs.text: To guarantee precision across multiple runs, your robot must establish clean baselines before launching.

docs.title: 1. Zeroing Wheel Motor Encoders
docs.text:
Technic motors measure their rotation relative to an internal optical encoder. As wheels spin, encoder degrees accumulate (\(360^\circ, 720^\circ, 1080^\circ \dots\)). * In Telemetry Dock: Open ⚙️ Motors and click ↺ Zero Encoders. All motor angles reset to \(0^\circ\). * In Python Code: 

from spike import Motor
motor_a = Motor('A')
motor_a.set_degrees_counted(0)

docs.title: 2. Calibrating Gyro IMU Heading
docs.text:
When the robot spawns, the Gyro yaw is aligned with the table coordinates. However, after making multiple complex turns, you may want to redefine the robot's current heading as \(0.0^\circ\): * In Telemetry Dock: Under the 🧭 Gyro / IMU Yaw card, click the 🧭 Zero button. The compass needle snaps to North (\(0^\circ\)). * In Python Code: 

from spike import PrimeHub
hub = PrimeHub()
hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()

docs.title: 🏆 Hands-On Challenge 4: Hardware Remapping & Dyno Attachment Test
Challenge Prompt:
docs.text:
Scenario: Your team's builder moved the robot's drive motors to Ports C and D, and mounted a dual-geared lifting fork on Port A.

Requirements: 1. Open the Robot Design & Hardware Port Inspector and remap: * Drive Left Wheel \(\to\) Port C * Drive Right Wheel \(\to\) Port D * Auxiliary Attachment 1 \(\to\) Port A 2. Save your port mapping. 3. Engage Dyno Jig Mode. 4. Write a Python test script that: * Drives the new wheels (Ports C & D) forward for 3 rotations to verify mapping. * Cycles the attachment fork on Port A: sweeps \(+90^\circ\) clockwise, pauses \(1.0\,\text{s}\), then sweeps \(-90^\circ\) counter-clockwise. 5. Confirm in the Telemetry Dock that: * Robot coordinates (X, Z) do not move (Dyno locked). * Wheel encoders on C & D show \(\approx 1080^\circ\) of rotation. * Attachment motor on A shows exactly \(0^\circ\) net rotation after completing the cycle.

docs.title: Challenge 4 Solution
docs.text:
Python Test Script (dyno_hardware_test.py)Word Blocks Stack 
from spike import MotorPair, Motor
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

print("=== CHALLENGE 4: DYNO ATTACHMENT BENCHMARK ===")

# 1. Initialize with remapped hardware ports
motors = MotorPair('C', 'D')  # Drive wheels remapped to C & D
fork_motor = Motor('A')       # Attachment arm remapped to A

# Configure speeds
motors.set_default_speed(50)
fork_motor.set_default_speed(40)

# 2. Benchmark Drive Motors in Dyno Jig
print("Testing remapped drive motors on Ports C & D (3 rotations = 1080°)...")
motors.move(3, 'rotations')
print("Drive motor benchmark complete.")

# 3. Benchmark Attachment Motor on Port A
print("Testing attachment arm on Port A: Sweeping +90°...")
fork_motor.run_for_degrees(90)

print("Holding position for 1.0s (inspecting gear mesh)...")
wait_for_seconds(1.0)

print("Returning attachment arm: Sweeping -90°...")
fork_motor.run_for_degrees(-90)

print("=== BENCHMARK SUCCESSFUL: HARDWARE MAPPING VERIFIED ===")

docs.title: Tutorial 5: 3D CAD Model Inspector & Studio 2.0 Digital Twins
docs.text:
In modern aerospace, automotive, and industrial engineering, machines are designed and tested as Digital Twins—virtual 3D replicas with realistic mass, joints, and physics—long before raw materials are cut or assembled.

In FIRST LEGO League, your team can achieve the same engineering rigor! With fll-sim's 3D CAD Model Inspector & Diagnostic Validator, you can import your team's custom robot builds directly from BrickLink Studio (.io) or LDraw (.ldr), analyze Topological Pin Clustering, test real-world season mission elements (such as M01 Coral Reef), and verify mechanism physics using virtual sandbox tools before deploying them to the competition mat.

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  1. Launch and navigate the 3D CAD Model Inspector & Diagnostic Validator.
  2. Understand the mathematics and algorithmic role of Topological Pin Clustering for 60 Hz real-time physics.
  3. Inspect robot submodels, center-of-mass coordinates, mass breakdowns, and kinematic joint limits.
  4. Load, inspect, and benchmark official Season Mission Models (e.g. M01 Coral Reef).
  5. Interact with simulated mechanisms using the Virtual Mouse Grab Hand and the Technic Push Bar.
  6. Deploy verified CAD models directly onto the 3D competition mat.
  7. Solve Hands-On Challenge 5 by verifying a mission model mechanism and creating an autonomous interaction script.

docs.title: 🔬 Step 1: Launching the CAD Model Inspector
docs.text:
You can open the CAD Inspector in two ways: 1. Click the 🔬 CAD Inspector button in the top navigation bar. 2. Open 🤖 Robot Design and click 🔬 Open in 3D CAD Inspector.

The full-screen inspection laboratory loads instantly:

docs.title: The CAD Inspector Interface Overview:
docs.text:
• Left Diagnostics Sidebar: Displays model metadata, part count breakdown, total mass calculation in grams, center of mass coordinates (X, Y, Z), and the submodel hierarchy tree.
  • Central 3D Interactive Viewport: Studio-grade lighting, millimeter grid floor, wireframe toggle, collider mesh visualizer, and orbital camera.
  • Top Navigation Bar: Model selector dropdown (custom robot uploads vs. official season mission models), Step Debugger playback controls, and the green 🚀 Deploy to Mat button.
  • Bottom Sandbox Toolbar: Physics run toggle (▶ Live Physics), 🖐️ Mouse Grab Hand, and 📏 Technic Push Bar.

docs.title: Why Can't Simulators Just Simulate Every LEGO Piece Individually?
docs.text:
A typical FLL competition robot contains between 130 and 350 individual LEGO Technic elements: beams, connector pins, cross-axles, bushings, and motor housings.

If a 3D physics engine (like Rapier 3D) attempted to simulate all 250 individual pieces connected by 500 loose contact joints every frame, two catastrophic problems would occur: 1. Computational Drag: The frame rate would collapse from 60 FPS down to 5 FPS. 2. Physics Jitter / Exploding Joints: Slight floating-point rounding errors would cause the robot's frame to wobble, vibrate, or tear itself apart on the virtual mat!

docs.title: The Solution: Topological Pin Clustering
docs.text:
fll-sim implements an advanced graph-theory algorithm called Topological Pin Clustering:

flowchart TD
    A["Raw CAD Input: 180+ Parts
(Beams, Axles, Friction Pins 2780, 6558)"] --> B["Kinematic Graph Solver
(Detects rigid friction pin connections)"]
    B --> C["Rigid Body Clustering
• Cluster 0: Consolidated Chassis Body
• Cluster 1: Left Wheel Rim & Tire
• Cluster 2: Right Wheel Rim & Tire
• Cluster 3: Motorized Arm Mechanism"]
    C --> D["Kinematic Joint Assignment
• Revolute Joint (Left Wheel Axle)
• Revolute Joint (Right Wheel Axle)
• Motor Actuator Joint (Attachment)"]
    D --> E["Rock-Solid 60 Hz Physics
(Zero Jitter, Exact Inertia Tensor)"]
  1. Graph Traversal: The solver examines every Technic friction pin (2780, 6558, 32054) and axle connector.
  2. Rigid Consolidation: Any parts rigidly bound to one another are consolidated into a single composite rigid body with compound collision boxes.
  3. Freedom Detection: When an axle passes through a smooth round hole (1 Degree-of-Freedom rotation), the solver automatically creates a Revolute Joint with realistic motor torque limits!
  4. Performance Result: Over 180 individual pieces are reduced to just 3 to 5 rigid bodies, running at an ultra-smooth 60 FPS!

docs.title: 📊 Step 3: Inspecting Robot Kinematics, Submodels, and Mass Calculation
docs.text: In the left diagnostics panel, inspect the physical properties computed for the Advanced Driving Base:

docs.title: 1. Mass Calculation & Center of Mass (CoM)
docs.text:
• Total Assembly Mass: \(474.8\,\text{g}\)
    • SPIKE Prime Hub: \(215.0\,\text{g}\)
    • Medium Motors (x2): \(144.0\,\text{g}\) (\(72\,\text{g}\) each)
    • Technic Beams & Frames: \(68.5\,\text{g}\)
    • Balloon Wheels & Tires (x2): \(32.0\,\text{g}\) (\(16\,\text{g}\) each)

Click the Show Colliders toggle in the top bar to visualize the purple compound bounding boxes wrapped around each component.

In the model selector dropdown in the top bar, choose M01: Coral Reef:

docs.title: The Coral Reef Kinematic Anatomy:
docs.text:
• Base Frame: Clustered into a static rigid body held securely to the field mat using simulated 3M Dual Lock fasteners.
  • Coral Lever Arm: Connected by a Technic cross-axle through a low-friction bush, allowing a \(60^\circ\) rotational sweep.
  • Counterweight / Latch: Includes realistic gravity physics—when pushed past its equilibrium tipping point (\(38^\circ\)), it drops into the scored position with an authentic mechanical latch!

docs.title: 🖐️ Step 5: Physical Sandbox Testing (Virtual Hand & Push Bar)
docs.text:
Before writing any autonomous code, you can test how the mission model behaves under physical forces!

Click ▶ Live Physics in the bottom toolbar to awaken the Rapier 3D simulation engine. Then test using the two interactive tools:

docs.title: 1. The Virtual Mouse Grab Hand (🖐️ Grab)
docs.text:

docs.title: 🏆 Hands-On Challenge 5: Digital Twin Verification & Mission Run
docs.text: Put your digital twin engineering skills to the test!

docs.title: Challenge Prompt:
docs.text:
Scenario: Your team is designing an autonomous run to actuate M01 Coral Reef.

Requirements: 1. Open the CAD Inspector and load M01 Coral Reef. 2. Enable ▶ Live Physics and use the Virtual Mouse Grab Hand to determine the tipping angle where the coral branch latches into the scored state. 3. Switch to the Technic Push Bar to verify that a forward push at \(35\,\text{mm}\) height successfully trips the latch. 4. Click 🚀 Deploy to Mat to place the verified model on the field. 5. Return to the Code Editor and write an autonomous Python run that drives the robot forward into the Coral Reef, pauses for latch confirmation, and backs away. 6. Record the drive distance and attachment bumper contact in your engineering notebook notes!

docs.title: Challenge 5 Solution
docs.text:
Python Autonomous Mission RunWord Blocks Stack 
from spike import PrimeHub, MotorPair
from spike.control import wait_for_seconds

# 1. Initialize Hub and Motors
hub = PrimeHub()
motors = MotorPair('A', 'B')

# Zero gyro
hub.motion_sensor.reset_yaw_angle()
wait_for_seconds(0.2)

print("=== M01 CORAL REEF AUTONOMOUS MISSION ===")

# 2. Set moderate cruising speed for high contact traction
motors.set_default_speed(40)

# 3. Drive forward 38.0 cm toward Coral Reef lever
print("Navigating to Coral Reef (38 cm)...")
motors.move(38, 'cm')

# 4. Low-speed push (push bar contacts lever at 35mm elevation)
print("Engaging push bar against mission lever...")
motors.move_tank(20, 20, left_speed=20, right_speed=20)
motors.move(6, 'cm')  # Extra 6 cm push to trip gravity latch

# 5. Brief stabilization pause
wait_for_seconds(0.5)
print("Coral Reef latch tripped and scored!")

# 6. Reverse back safely to Home Base
print("Reversing back to Red Launch Arc...")
motors.move(-44, 'cm')

print("=== MISSION 1 COMPLETE: SCORE RECORDED ===")

docs.title: 🖥️ UI Components & Global Controls Reference
docs.text:
The FLL Robot Simulator (fll-sim) features an authentic, competition-grade web graphical interface engineered specifically for FIRST® LEGO® League teams, mentors, and students. Built with Three.js (WebGL), Rapier3D physics (WebAssembly), and an authentic SPIKE™ Prime execution runtime, the simulator combines real-time 3D simulation with modular telemetry, interactive Scratch Word Blocks, Python programming, and CAD inspection.

This reference provides an exhaustive guide to every UI component, modal dialog, control surface, docking mode, telemetry feed, and keyboard shortcut available in the simulator.

docs.title: Primary Layout Zones
docs.text:
1. Top Navigation Bar (.hud-topbar): Always-visible 48px header containing brand identity, execution status, match countdown timer, camera angle presets, active program selector, script execution triggers (RUN, STOP, RESET), and modal quick-launch icons.
  2. 3D Competition Mat Viewport (#viewport-container): High-performance Three.js WebGL rendering canvas simulating official 2362mm × 1143mm competition mats with physically accurate lighting, friction surfaces, drop reticles, and live robot kinematics.
  3. Dockable & Minimizable Telemetry Pane (#hud-telemetry-dock): Flexible diagnostics pane supporting horizontal bottom docking, vertical right docking, or a 30px minimized status bar. Houses live sensor meters, motor velocity cards, and real-time physics event logs.
  4. Left Activity Bar (.hud-activity-bar): Fixed 48px vertical rail providing single-click switching between functional workspaces: Code, Manual Driver, Asset Library, Fasteners, Field Setup, and Debug Terminal.
  5. Left Resizable Multi-Job Drawer (#hud-drawer-panel): Sliding secondary workspace resizable between 380px and 760px. Hosts embedded script editors, WASD manual driving, mission catalog loaders, and layout persistence controls.

Workspace Customization

All panels in the simulator can be resized, collapsed, or popped out into floating modals. On multi-monitor or widescreen displays, open the Code Editor and CAD Inspector in dedicated modal overlays while keeping the 3D Mat Viewport full-width.

docs.title: 3. 3D Competition Mat Viewport & Camera Navigation
docs.text: The 3D Competition Mat Viewport renders the physical competition table with millimeter accuracy, simulating official FLL mat dimensions (2362 mm × 1143 mm) bounded by rigid Baltic birch borders.

docs.title: Camera Perspectives & Orbit Navigation
docs.text:
The Three.js viewport provides three specialized camera modes:

Top-Down View (Default)Isometric 3D ViewDynamic Follow Camera
  • Optimal For: Line alignment, path planning, launch angle measurement, and 2D odometry tracking.
  • Camera Orientation: Positioned directly over field center (0.0, 2.5, 0.0) looking straight down with locked pitch.
  • Reticle Interaction: Drag the robot or mission models smoothly along the X/Z ground plane.
  • Optimal For: Inspecting attachment clearance, vertical mission levers, gear meshing, and 3D collisions.
  • Camera Orientation: 45° azimuth, 35° elevation angled view showing depth and elevation profiles.
  • Shadow & Depth: Directional shadow maps highlight ground clearance and tire contact patches.
  • Optimal For: Long-distance navigation runs, obstacle traversal, and driver-perspective missions.
  • Tracking Dynamics: Automatically tracks the robot chassis centroid, maintaining an offset distance while damping high-frequency vibrations.

docs.title: Interactive Viewport Controls
docs.text:
• Orbit Rotate: Click and drag with ++left-button-click++ across the mat surface to orbit around the current focus target.
  • Pan Camera: Click and drag with ++right-button-click++ (or ++ctrl+left-button-click++) to translate the camera target across the mat.
  • Smooth Zoom: Scroll mouse wheel (++wheel-up++ / ++wheel-down++) or pinch-to-zoom on touchpads.
  • Object Placement & Dragging: Click and hold on the robot or any unlocked mission element to enter positioning mode. A cyan drop reticle projects the exact ground footprint.
  • Keyboard In-Place Rotation: While hovering or dragging any object, press ++r++ (clockwise +15°) or ++shift+r++ (counter-clockwise -15°) to rotate in place without moving coordinates.

docs.title: Dynamic 3D Compass & Heading Indicator
docs.text: Positioned in the 3D viewport and telemetry cards, the dynamic compass renders: * North Needle (Crimson Red): Real-time absolute field alignment. * Digital Yaw Heading: Live precision degrees with clockwise positive convention (0.0° to 359.9° or ±180°). * Heading Zero Button (🧭 Zero): Instantly resets the internal IMU software offset to 0.0° relative to the robot's current heading.

docs.title: 4. Dockable & Minimizable Telemetry Pane
docs.text: The Telemetry Pane provides real-time visibility into internal robot state, optical sensors, distance sonars, motor tachometers, and Rapier3D physics collision logs.

docs.title: Flexible Docking Configurations
docs.text:
The telemetry system supports three distinct operational layouts to fit any screen aspect ratio:

  • Zero Button: Instant recalibration to zero without altering physical position.

docs.text:
• Coordinates Grid: Live tracking of chassis center of mass:
  • X: Millimeters from arena center line (-1.18 m to +1.18 m).
  • Z: Millimeters from arena south edge (-0.57 m to +0.57 m).
  • Yaw: Heading angle in degrees.
  • 📌 Capture Pose: Click to save the robot's current position and rotation as the new starting spawn point.

docs.title: Motor Diagnostics Cards (Ports A–F)
docs.text:
Each motor port card (A, B, C, D, E, F) renders real-time mechanical parameters:

  • Drive Motors (Ports A & B): Left and right drive wheels configured with differential kinematics.
  • Auxiliary Motors (Ports C–F): Medium and large angled motors driving mission manipulators, rack-and-pinion pushers, and gearboxes.
  • Telemetry Fields:
  • Target Power / Speed: Programmed velocity setpoint (-100% to +100%).
  • Actual Angular Velocity: Real-time velocity reported in both degrees per second (°/s) and revolutions per minute (RPM).
  • Cumulative Encoder Angle: High-precision rotary tachometer reading with zeroing action (↺ Zero).

docs.title: Live Command & Physics Event Logs Stream
docs.text:
The right column of the telemetry dock streams real-time communication events between the Python runtime and the Rapier3D physics solver:

  • Category Filter Pills:
  • All: Full execution transcript.
  • Drive: Movement commands (move(), steer(), start_tank()).
  • Brake: Mechanical stopping events (stop(), active holding torque).
  • Motors: Individual auxiliary motor actions (run_for_degrees(), run_to_position()).
  • Log Controls:
  • Auto-scroll Checkbox: Automatically pins view to newest events.
  • 🧹 Clear Logs: Empties memory buffer and clears log console.
  • Performance Badge: Live pulsing badge displaying Three.js rendering frame rate (60 FPS) and physics engine frequency (60 Hz). Clicking opens the Performance Profiler.

docs.text: Hover over the right vertical border of the drawer panel (#hud-panel-resizer) to reveal the horizontal resize cursor. Click and drag horizontally to resize anywhere between 380px and 760px width. The 3D viewport canvas automatically resizes with zero aspect ratio distortion.

docs.title: Manual Driver Mode (WASD & Motors)
docs.text: Manual Driver Mode allows operators to manually steer the robot and test mission mechanisms using direct keyboard inputs:

docs.title: 1. Drive Base Controls (WASD)
docs.text:
• ++w++: Drive straight forward at configured speed.
  • ++s++: Drive straight backward in reverse.
  • ++a++: Spin counter-clockwise in place (left motor reverse, right motor forward).
  • ++d++: Spin clockwise in place (left motor forward, right motor reverse).
  • ++space++: Instant emergency brake (both drive motors locked).
  • Speed Slider (10% – 100%): Sets baseline velocity for WASD driving actions.

docs.title: 2. Individual Motor Keybindings (UIOP / JKL;)
docs.text:
Drive auxiliary attachments and individual motors directly from keyboard key pairs:

Motor Port Forward Key Reverse Key Default Role Port A ++u++ ++j++ Left Drive Wheel Port B ++i++ ++k++ Right Drive Wheel Port C ++o++ ++l++ Left Auxiliary Motor / Arm Port D ++p++ ++;++ Right Auxiliary Motor / Arm

Focus Safety

When typing inside code textareas, file input modals, or rename inputs, the driver mode automatically disarms key listeners to prevent accidental robot movement.

docs.title: 6. SPIKE Prime Word Blocks Studio & Python Editor
docs.text: The code editor provides a complete, authentic FIRST LEGO League programming environment with full parity between Scratch-based Word Blocks and official SPIKE Prime Python code.
